title: Introduction to symbolic logic
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn formal logic as philosophers use it: truth-functional logic (symbolization, truth tables and natural deduction) and first-order logic with quantifiers, identity and relations (symbolization, interpretations and countermodels, and natural deduction proofs), with the ideas of soundness and completeness.
primary_reading: forall x: Calgary, an open introduction to formal logic (free)

weeks.3: Truth tables: tautologies, entailment and equivalence
weeks.6: Natural deduction: conditional proof, indirect proof and strategy
weeks.7: First-order logic: names, predicates and quantifiers
weeks.9: Identity, definite descriptions and numerical claims
weeks.12: Soundness and completeness: what they say and why they matter

blocks.deliverable: Test eight arguments with complete or partial truth tables.
Write ten proofs in truth-functional logic.
Week 7 midterm; symbolize ten sentences with nested quantifiers.
Build countermodels for five invalid arguments.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Logic workbook: formalize five arguments from classic philosophical texts (for example an ontological argument, a skeptical argument and an argument about personal identity), prove the valid ones in natural deduction, give countermodels for the invalid ones, and write a page on what formalizing each argument revealed.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
